note: Fictional story. Every character, company, newspaper and broadcast in it is invented and none depicts a real person. The city issues it plays with are real.

prologue.t: Everett, Washington. My dad made paper here for thirty one years.
Then the mill closed. The city put a fence around it and called it an opportunity.
I left for eight years. Came back with a duffel bag and a car that is not mine.
Dee got me a job driving packages. Dee always gets me a job. Dee is the reason I ever left, and the reason I came back.
First call I got was from the library. Nobody calls from the library with good news.

epilogue.t: They did not cancel the ballpark. They tabled it. In this town, that counts as a miracle.
Pruitt still owns half of downtown. Sam prints the news in his garage. Olsen talks now. Loudly.
The library is open Sundays. Marge says I still owe for the book.
Everett is not broke, Danny. It was spending on the wrong things.

chapters.title: WELCOME BACK

intro.t: Ninety one minutes.
Ninety is the limit.
I can pay the ticket.
Can't release it. Your tabs are expired.
I can't renew the tabs. There are toll penalties on the plate.
So pay those.
With the job I can't drive to.
Mister Pruitt is hiring. Commerce Building, on Hewitt. You'll have to walk.

steps.text: Your car is booted. Walk to Pruitt's office at the Commerce Building

outro.t: You know what a parking meter is, Danny? It is a clock that pays me when it stops.
The city runs the meters.
The city runs the street. I run everywhere you go when the street says no.

chapters.news: Port Gardner Radio news. Downtown parking: experts say ninety minutes is plenty, if you know what you want.

chapters.title: 90 MINUTES

intro.t: Cars on Wetmore and Colby are about to hit ninety minutes. I want them in my lot before the owners finish lunch.
And my car?
The boot comes off when you bring me two. Take whatever is over the limit.

steps.text: A wagon by the theatre plaza just ran over ninety minutes. Take it

done.t: Ninety one minutes. That one is mine now.

steps.text: Drive it to Pruitt's impound lot at Everett Downtown Storage
One more. A sedan outside the library is over the limit

done.t: Somebody is going to come out of that library very unhappy.

steps.text: Bring the sedan to the impound lot

outro.t: That is my car. I was returning books. The library closes at five now. Did you know that?
I just drive the truck.
Everybody just drives the truck, honey.

chapters.news: Port Gardner Radio news. Tow volumes are up forty percent. City Hall calls it a sign of a busy downtown.

chapters.title: OVERDUE

intro.t: Danny Voss. You still owe us for a book on engine repair. Nineteen ninety eight.
I fixed the engine.
They cut our hours again. Closed Sundays, closed Mondays. The same week they found millions for a ballpark.
What do you want me to do about it, Marge?
I have been back two days. I drive packages for Dee.
Your father read every Zane Grey we had. Twice. He would not let them lock that door without a fight.
Four thousand signatures. The clerk locks the door at five. You drive like your father. So drive.

steps.text: Get the petitions to City Hall before the clerk leaves

radio.t: Danny, it's Dee. City Hall, Wetmore side. And slow down, I can hear your tires from dispatch.
Good to hear your voice too, Dee.

outro.t: Did they take them?
Stamped and filed.
Good. Now they have to pretend to read them.

post.t: Four thousand signatures. About a library.
Mayor, nobody ever cut a ribbon on a library being open on a Sunday.
I want that ballpark open by spring, Lyle.

chapters.news: Port Gardner Radio news. Library hours are cut again as the city faces a budget gap. Officials say the downtown ballpark is still on schedule.

chapters.title: DEMOLITION BY NEGLECT

intro.t: See that cornice? Nineteen twenty five. Lyle Pruitt bought the block, pulled the tenants, and left the windows open all winter.
Why would a man wreck his own building?
Because a ruin is cheaper to tear down than a landmark. They call it demolition by neglect. We call it Tuesday.
Three notices. Culmback, Commerce, McCabe. Once it is posted, it is on the record.

steps.text: Post a notice on the Culmback Building (1/3)

radio.t: A staple gun and a ladder. This is what I came home for.

steps.text: Post a notice on the Commerce Building (2/3)
Post a notice on the McCabe Building (3/3)

lines.t: Son, you are stapling paper to my property.
Everything is public until somebody buys it. Lyle Pruitt. I am the reason this town is going to have a skyline.
Tell Marge I said hello. And tell her winter is coming.

outro.t: He came down and talked to you himself?
White hat. Big smile.
Then we are finally doing something right.
Marge. Why do you care this much about old brick?
Because I taught half this town to read in rooms like those. You tear down the room, people forget they were ever in it.

chapters.news: Preservation notices appeared overnight on three downtown buildings owned by developer Lyle Pruitt. Pruitt called it vandalism with paperwork.

chapters.title: BALLPARK FIGURE

intro.t: Sam Reyes, Everett Ledger. I am the newsroom. All of it.
Marge said you needed a driver.
What happened to the rest of it?
Bought, sold, and laid off. I kept the keys because nobody asked for them back.
I need a number. The ballpark had a price. Then it had a bigger one. Nobody will show me the estimate.
The contractor keeps the binders in a box truck by the station. I am a reporter. I can't steal a truck.
But you can ask me to.
I would call it sourcing.

steps.text: Take the contractor's box truck near Everett Station

done.t: Danny. That is not your truck.

steps.text: Bring the truck to the Ledger office at the Evergreen Building

outro.t: Look at this. A new total every month, and every one of them stamped final.
Where is the extra going?
That is the story. Somebody is selling the city the dirt under home plate. Guess who owns the dirt.

chapters.news: The Everett Ledger reports the ballpark estimate has grown by tens of millions. Mayor Dale Hargrove calls the number, quote, a rough ballpark figure.

post.t: Somebody took a truck, Lyle. With your binders in it.
Binders are paper, Mayor. Paper burns, paper gets lost, paper gets explained.
You ran on a ballpark. I am just the man who knows what it costs.

chapters.title: RIBBON CUTTING

intro.t: You're the driver? Wonderful. Whit Brannigan, your congressman. I am late for three ribbons.
Three.
A bus shelter, a crane, and a hot dog stand at the arena. Federal dollars at work.
I have a truck full of borrowed binders on my mind, sir.
I did not hear that. I never hear anything. It is how I have lasted.

steps.text: Drive the congressman to Everett Station (1/3)

radio.t: Faster. No, slower, there is a camera. Wave!

steps.text: Now the Port of Everett (2/3)

radio.t: Between us. Lyle Pruitt asked my office for federal money for that ballpark. I said, send the paperwork. He never did.
Men with clean deals love paperwork.

steps.text: Last ribbon: Angel of the Winds Arena (3/3)

radio.t: You know what I admire about ribbons? They cannot be audited.
I'm starting to see why you last.

outro.t: You never drove me. But if you had, you were excellent.
Yes sir.
And son? Whatever is in those binders. Read the last page first.

chapters.news: Congressman Whit Brannigan cut three ribbons in under six minutes today. His office is calling it a district record.

chapters.title: EYES ON BROADWAY

intro.t: They fired me this morning. Pruitt bought the Ledger's building. New landlord, new priorities.
So it's over.
I still have a login. The city hung plate cameras on every road into town. Somebody ran a search on Marge's car. And on yours.
Who?
The audit log says who. It is at the service center, on paper, because nobody trusts the system that watches everybody.

steps.text: Pick up the audit at the City Service Center

done.t: Danny, every camera on Broadway just lit up with your plate. They are coming.

steps.text: The cameras saw you. Lose the police

done.t: You're clear. I don't know how. Do not tell me how.

steps.text: Bring the audit back to Sam at the courthouse

outro.t: The searches came from a contractor account. Pruitt Development. He is using the city's cameras like a doorbell.
Can you print it?
I don't have a paper anymore. I have a printer.
Danny Voss. Every man in this town has a number. I am calling to ask yours.
My dad's was thirty one years. You could not afford him either.

chapters.news: Questions tonight about who can see the city's license plate camera logs. The police chief says the system is working as intended.

chapters.title: STRUCTURAL DEFICIT

intro.t: Your old man loaded pulp on this dock. He would hate what I am about to tell you.
Pruitt has been paying me to move cars out through the old mill site. Tonight it is a gold coupe with a trunk that sits low.
Cash.
The kind that never saw a bank. The kind that buys a vote before a meeting.
Why tell me?
They closed the mill and I said nothing. I am done saying nothing.

steps.text: Take Pruitt's gold coupe at the old mill site

done.t: That is my car, son. Bring it back and I will forget your face.
You already ran my plate. You know exactly who I am.

steps.text: Get the coupe to Marge at the library in one piece

outro.t: Good lord. How much is in there?
Enough to keep the lights on Sundays for about a hundred years.
I shelved books in this building for forty years. Nobody ever brought me a trunk.
We cannot keep it, Danny.
No. But we can bring it to the meeting and ask the mayor whose it is.

chapters.news: Developer Lyle Pruitt reports a gold coupe stolen from the old mill site. He declined to say what was in the trunk.

chapters.title: PUBLIC COMMENT

intro.t: The council votes at seven. Three minutes at the microphone. That is all a citizen gets.
I have the binders, the audit, and a trunk of cash with his name on the bands.
Then you do the talking.
No. They have heard me for forty years. They have never heard you.

steps.text: Get to City Hall before the vote. Every cop in town is looking for you

radio.t: The whole department is looking for you, Danny. You picked a real quiet night.

lines.t: You are the driver. I was born here too, son. Colby Avenue. I wanted to build one thing before I am done.
Then build the thing we asked you for.
It never is, until somebody says it out loud. I am about to say it out loud.
It's six fifty eight. Danny Voss. Born on Rucker, raised on Rockefeller.
My dad worked the mill. When it closed, you told us there was no money. No money for the library. No money for the old buildings. No money for anything that was already ours.
Here is the estimate you never showed us. Here is who has been running our plates. And here is a trunk of cash from the man who sells you the dirt.
No sir. Theater is the ribbon cuttings. This is public comment.
The chair moves to table the vote.

outro.t: Three minutes. You used two.
I ran out of things to say.
No you didn't. You just said them once.

chapters.news: A surprise at City Hall tonight. The council tabled the ballpark vote after public comment ran four hours. Mayor Hargrove says he looks forward to further study.
